item.title: Liver biopsy confirms precise and efficient correction of SERPINA1 after in vivo Base Editing in a Patient with Alpha-1 Antitrypsin Deficiency.
item.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency (AATD) caused by the PI*ZZ genotype (Glu342Lys) is characterized by hepatic accumulation of misfolded AAT-Z protein and reduced circulating AAT levels, leading to progressive liver disease and pulmonary emphysema. Gene correction therapy represents a potentially curative approach by directly correcting the underlying genetic defect. We report the first clinical case with direct assessment of hepatic gene correction by liver biopsy following in vivo base editing in a patient with AATD.
METHODS/CASE PRESENTATION: We report the case of a 66-year-old male patient with PI*ZZ AATD who underwent gene correction therapy within the YOLT-202 phase I/Ia clinical trial (clinical trial.gov ID NCT07193615). Ten weeks after treatment a liver biopsy was performed to assess hepatic histology in the context of pre-existing F2 fibrosis identified by elastography before treatment. Liver tissue was analyzed for correction of the Pi*ZZ variant using Sanger and Illumina sequencing, including assessment of bystander and off-target editing. Serum levels and biological activity of AAT were assessed longitudinally using an elastase inhibition assay.
RESULTS: Liver biopsy showed no evidence of hepatic inflammation and demonstrated correction of the PI*ZZ variant in 54% of alleles by Sanger and 57% by Illumina sequencing without detectable off-target signals. Following a transient post-treatment increase in transaminases, liver enzymes returned to baseline. Monthly measurements demonstrated sustained circulating AAT levels with preserved biological activity, as assessed by elastase inhibition, throughout follow-up.
CONCLUSIONS: In vivo base editing achieved substantial and precise hepatic correction of the pathogenic SERPINA1 PI*ZZ variant, without concerning histological findings or detectable bystander or off-target editing. Sustained biologically active AAT levels support feasibility and potential of this approach for the treatment of AATD.

item.title: Research progress in the production, purification, and applications of long single-stranded DNA.
item.abstract: Long single-stranded DNA (long ssDNA) plays important roles in cutting-edge fields such as DNA origami, gene therapy, and synthetic biology. However, the production, preparation, and purification of long ssDNA remain technically challenging. This review systematically summarizes current strategies for long ssDNA production and preparation, including phage-E. coli-based biological production, template-dependent enzymatic amplification, and viral-vector-based generation of ssDNA genomes. CRISPR-Cas-assisted approaches are discussed separately as complementary tools for post-synthetic processing, sequence-selective cleavage, enrichment, and quality control, whereas other enzymatic approaches are considered for post-synthetic strand conversion. We compare the characteristics and limitations of these production and preparation strategies, discuss purification techniques for long ssDNA, and summarize its applications in DNA origami nanotechnology and gene therapy. This review comprehensively synthesizes the bottlenecks in long ssDNA production, preparation, and purification, and outlines further development trends. We highlight template-independent de novo enzymatic DNA synthesis, automated DNA manufacturing, synthetic biology-based production systems, and AI-assisted sequence optimization. These developments are expected to accelerate the transition of long ssDNA technologies from laboratory research toward scalable manufacturing and practical applications.

item.title: Self-organization of Drosophila chromatin architecture in a cell-free system.
item.abstract: Metazoan genomes are organized by folding of the nucleosome fiber into loops and domains that support long-range regulatory interactions. Although cohesin-mediated loop extrusion and architectural DNA-binding proteins are central to current models of genome organization, how these mechanisms integrate to generate higher-order structure remains incompletely understood. Early Drosophila melanogaster embryogenesis provides a unique window into the emergence of chromatin architecture, as rapid syncytial nuclear divisions occur largely in the absence of transcription. However, probing the mechanisms underlying this primordial folding in vivo is technically challenging. Here, we establish an in vitro system that reconstitutes complex chromatin using extracts from syncytial embryos. Nucleosome mapping and Micro-C analyses reveal that long-range interactions, including cis and trans loops and topologically associating domains (TADs), emerge spontaneously from soluble extract components. While some structures resemble those observed in early embryos, others represent latent interaction potentials that are constrained in vivo. Focusing on the eve locus, we find that TAD formation is incompatible with a simple loop extrusion model and instead requires direct pairing of boundary elements mediated by the insulator protein 'Suppressor-of-hairy-wing' Su(Hw). Together, our work demonstrates that key features of 3D genome organization can be reconstituted in a cell-free system and provides a tractable platform for the mechanistic dissection of chromatin folding in Drosophila.

item.title: CRISPR/Cas9-based Genome Editing in Inherited Diseases: Mechanisms, Therapeutic Advances, Safety and Clinical Translation.
item.abstract: Gene therapy has transformed modern biomedical research by enabling curative strategies that target the molecular basis of disease. Among genome-editing technologies, the CRISPR/Cas9 system has emerged as a versatile and efficient platform due to its programmability, simplicity, and precision. This review summarizes the evolution of gene therapy and highlights the therapeutic potential of CRISPR-based genome editing. CRISPR/Cas9 has demonstrated significant potential in correcting disease-causing mutations across multiple inherited disorders, including sickle cell disease, β- thalassemia, familial hypercholesterolemia, phenylketonuria, muscular dystrophies, and cystic fibrosis. Emerging technologies such as base editing and prime editing further improved editing precision and reduced unintended genomic alterations. However, challenges including off-target effects, DNA repair pathway bias, immune responses, and vector-associated toxicities remain major limitations. The review highlights the rapid progress of CRISPR-mediated therapeutics and emphasizes the importance of improving editing accuracy, delivery efficiency, and long-term safety. Advances in vector engineering and genome-editing platforms are expected to overcome current technical and ethical barriers, facilitating broader clinical applications. CRISPR/Cas9 and related genome- editing technologies represent promising disease-modifying and potentially curative therapeutic approaches. Continued optimization of precision, safety, and delivery systems will be essential for successful translation into routine clinical practice.

item.title: Harnessing yeast biodiversity to identify superior chassis strains for metabolic engineering and precision fermentation.
item.abstract: Microbial cell factories are increasingly used for the sustainable production of fuels, chemicals and pharmaceuticals. Yeasts are particularly suitable as production hosts because of their metabolic flexibility, robustness, and expanding synthetic biology toolkits. Metabolic engineering of yeast historically relied on a narrow set of reference species and strains, especially Saccharomyces cerevisiae. Recent studies, however, show that applying identical pathway designs to different strain backgrounds or species can yield significant differences in titer, rate and yield (TRY). In this review, we examine how diversity within and between species in genomic features, metabolic regulation, substrate utilization and stress tolerance shapes chassis performance. We focus on eight species, including S. cerevisiae, Yarrowia lipolytica, Kluyveromyces marxianus, Komagataella phaffii, Ogataea polymorpha, Rhodotorula toruloides, Lipomyces starkeyi and Pichia kudriavzevii. We highlight that different species and strain backgrounds provide distinct advantages depending on the target product, pathway requirements, substrate, and process conditions. Finally, we discuss the transition from empirical strain screening toward diversity-informed and predictive chassis selection through multi-omics, phenotyping, metabolic modeling, and machine learning. We propose that chassis identity should be treated as a design variable, and that chassis selection should become an integral part of the Design-Build-Test-Learn cycle to develop optimal cell factories.

item.title: Coacervate droplets as a liquefier for the solid-to-liquid transition of RNA aggregates.
item.abstract: Biomolecular condensates are functionally gated by their material properties. While RNA is a primary structural scaffold, its sequence-specific interactions can aberrantly drive condensates into dysfunctional solid aggregates. Yet, actively reversing this solidification to restore function remains a fundamental challenge, impeding progress in synthetic biology and therapeutics interventions. Here, we establish that complex coacervates can be engineered as liquefiers to actively remodel solid RNA-peptide aggregates into functional liquid droplets. Integrating systematic experiments with all-atom simulations, we decode a multiscale mechanism: coacervate infiltration at the micrometer scale mediates molecular buffering at the nanometer scale, which fluidizes the crosslinked network to drive macroscopic liquefaction. This capability is governed by a design rule, where coacervates formed by small-molecular anions exhibit optimal efficacy. We deploy this principle to functionally rescue silenced RNA within a model of pathologically solidified ribonucleoprotein assemblies. Our work provides a general framework for the active, compositional control of biomolecular phase behavior, with direct implications for managing pathological aggregation and engineering functional condensates in synthetic and living systems.
item.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America

item.title: Neural Stem Cell Therapies for Central Nervous System Regeneration: Advances, Challenges, and Integrative Technologies.
item.abstract: Neural stem cells (NSCs) are promising candidates for central nervous system (CNS) regeneration because they self-renew and differentiate into neural lineages. Advances in genome engineering, extracellular vesicles (EVs), biomaterials, organoids, single-cell technologies, and precision medicine have expanded approaches for characterizing, engineering, delivering, and evaluating NSC-based therapies for neurological disorders. CRISPR/Cas9 and related platforms may enable more precise modification of NSC function, while NSC-derived EVs offer potential cell-free strategies. Engineered hydrogels and three-dimensional scaffolds may improve cell survival, engraftment, migration, and integration. Organoids and single-cell omics provide increasingly detailed models of cellular heterogeneity and lineage specification. However, clinical translation remains limited by immune compatibility, tumorigenic risk, manufacturing standardization, graft survival and integration, and regulatory requirements. Rigorous preclinical validation, standardized manufacturing, appropriately designed clinical trials, long-term safety monitoring, and harmonized regulatory frameworks are required before routine clinical application.

item.title: Rising cell-free DNA level tracks cancer-associated methylation signal and improves multicancer detection.
item.abstract: Cancer patients carry more circulating cell-free DNA (ccfDNA)-small DNA fragments shed into the blood-than healthy people. Most of this excess comes not from the tumor itself but from immune cells, suggesting that it would simply dilute the much smaller amount of tumor-derived DNA in a blood sample. Using a study of 1,480 previously untreated participants across 43 hospitals-including patients with 14 cancer types spanning all stages, patients with benign growths, and healthy volunteers-we show the opposite: as total ccfDNA rises, it becomes enriched, not diluted, in fragments carrying cancer-associated DNA methylation signatures, independent of cancer type, disease stage, and a broad panel of demographic, clinical, and technical covariates. In fact, total ccfDNA explains more variance in cancer-associated methylation signal than the disease stage itself. This basic biological finding suggests a coupling between immune cell activity and tumor methylation. It also has a practical implication: we show that rising ccfDNA concentration is associated with higher cancer detection sensitivity, even within disease stages and particularly in early-stage disease-stage I sensitivity varied from 0.55 in the lowest ccfDNA concentration tertile to 0.85 in the highest, and stage II from 0.59 to 0.86. This suggests that ccfDNA concentration should be considered as a stage-independent stratification variable for benchmarking cancer-detection tests. Interestingly, similar behavior was observed in patients with symptomatic benign lesions, suggesting a broader biological response to abnormal tissue growth and not something unique to malignancy.
item.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America

item.title: LM2KM: feature extraction from pretrained protein and molecular language models combined with quantum mechanics (QM) features for K M predictions.
item.abstract: The Michaelis constant (K M) is a key parameter for characterizing enzyme-substrate interactions and plays an essential role in enzyme kinetics modeling and physiologically based pharmacokinetic (PBPK) applications. However, experimental determination of K M is labor-intensive, and existing computational prediction approaches remain limited in accuracy and scalability. In this study, we systematically evaluated pretrained protein and molecule language models for K M prediction by integrating four protein language models (PLMs) and two molecule language models (MLMs) to encode enzyme sequences and substrate structures, respectively. Principal component analysis (PCA) was applied to reduce feature dimensionality, and a wide range of representation combinations were assessed. Our results indicated that protein representations derived from the last four layers of ProtT5 using approximately 70 features, combined with 20 CLS-based molecular features from MolFormer, provided a well-balanced and efficient representation for K M prediction. In addition, the incorporation of quantum mechanics (QM) descriptors consistently improved prediction performance across all tested configurations, with the model R 2 of 0.537. In summary, this work provides a flexible and extensible framework for large-scale K M prediction, with strong potential to facilitate enzyme pathway identification, drug and lead screening, and sequence-based protein design, supporting broader applications in enzyme kinetics-driven modeling and drug development.

item.title: Deletion of the Envelope gene attenuates SARS-CoV-2 infection by altered spike localization and increased cell-to-cell transmission.
item.abstract: Severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) causes COVID-19, a highly transmissible acute respiratory infection that can result in severe pneumonia and death. Many details of SARS-CoV-2 infection are not fully understood, including the cell biology and host-virus interactions involved in coronavirus assembly and release, in which the Envelope (E) structural protein is instrumental. Deletion of E in other coronaviruses has been shown previously to either attenuate or abrogate infection. To determine the role of E in SARS-CoV-2 virus production and infectivity, we produced a reporter SARS-CoV-2 with or without the E gene deleted using a bacterial artificial chromosome. Replication of ΔE SARS-CoV-2 was attenuated in Vero E6 cells expressing human ACE2 and TMPRSS2 and in human epithelial cell lines. Electron and immunofluorescence microscopy and virology assays showed that ΔE SARS-CoV-2 increased cell surface expression of Spike (S) glycoprotein, leading to reduced S incorporation into ΔE SARS-CoV-2 particles and promotion of increased cell-to-cell transmission that evades neutralizing antibody inhibition. Trans-complementation of E partially rescued ΔE SARS-CoV-2 S incorporation and restored cell-free transmission. In addition to validating the role of E in retention of S in the ER-Golgi intermediate complex (ERGIC), our results showed that a lack of E led to reorganization of the ERGIC and Golgi during SARS-CoV-2 infection. Improved understanding of E in SARS-CoV-2 replication and host pathogenesis may help the development of novel therapeutics.IMPORTANCENon-Spike coronavirus structural proteins, including Envelope, are conserved, making them potential pan-coronavirus therapeutic targets. Many details about these proteins and their roles in viral replication and host pathogenesis are unknown. In this study, we showed that severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) replicates without Envelope but is attenuated and impaired in virus particle formation, with less Spike incorporated into virions and more Spike expressed on the cell surface compared to wild-type virus. SARS-CoV-2 lacking Envelope transmitted primarily via cell fusion and evaded neutralizing antibodies. In addition, the absence of Envelope resulted in the reorganization of the cell secretory compartment during SARS-CoV-2 infection. A better understanding of how Envelope influences SARS-CoV-2 replication could guide directed design of novel therapeutics for treatment of COVID-19 patients, as well as the potential for pan-coronavirus protection against future coronavirus outbreaks.

item.title: Cyclotides from Clitoria ternatea: Genomic Organization, Biosynthesis, and Roles in Plant Defense.
item.abstract: Clitoria ternatea, commonly known as butterfly pea, is a perennial legume widely recognized for its ornamental and medicinal value. Beyond its characteristic anthocyanin-rich blue flowers, the plant produces cyclotides, a type of ultra-stable, cyclic cystine-knot peptide, with exceptional biological functions. Unlike other cyclotide-bearing families that carry independent cyclotide genes, C. ternatea integrates cyclotide domains into albumin-1 genes, replacing β-chain domains through divergent or convergent evolution. Genomic and transcriptomic studies reveal a large repertoire of albumin-1 loci and associated biosynthetic enzymes, including asparaginyl endopeptidases (butelase-1), protein disulphide isomerases, and peptidyl-prolyl isomerases, which orchestrate the cyclization, folding, and stabilization of cyclotides. Transcriptome analyses further demonstrate tissue-specific expression patterns, with distinct cyclotides such as cliotides T2 and T3 enriched in flowers and pods, and cliotides T8-T10 specialized in seeds, reflecting adaptive responses to localized biotic stress. Functionally, C. ternatea cyclotides exhibit broad-spectrum defense properties, including insecticidal, bactericidal, nematicidal, and antifungal activities, primarily through membrane permeabilization and disruption of lipid bilayers. Their preferential affinity for phosphatidylethanolamine-rich membranes highlights their selective toxicity toward insect and microbial targets. Recent advances in synthetic biology exploit cyclotides' structural stability as molecular scaffolds for therapeutic peptide design, with applications in immunomodulatory, antimicrobial, and anticancer drug development. This review consolidates genomic, transcriptomic, and functional insights into cyclotide biosynthesis and activity in C. ternatea, highlighting its evolutionary distinctiveness and biotechnological potential. Future research integrating multi-omics and spatial single-cell analyses can further unravel regulatory networks, defense dynamics, and translational applications of these unique plant peptides.

item.title: Cell-Based Therapeutic Strategies for Correcting Mitochondrial DNA Mutations and Mitigating Oxidative Stress.
item.abstract: Mitochondria are essential structures that produce energy in cells through mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation and are one of the primary sources of reactive oxygen species (ROS). Mutations in mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) cause a wide range of hereditary illnesses with multisystem clinical symptoms, poor cellular bioenergetics, and decreased mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation. Effective treatment approaches have been hampered by the genetic complexity associated with mtDNA disorders, including heteroplasmy and tissue-specific diversity. The relationship between mutations in the mitochondrial DNA and oxidative stress is multidimensional and snowballing, with structural malfunction of the electron transport chain encouraging the development of ROS that causes further damage to mitochondrial DNA, lipids, and proteins. Under carefully regulated experimental conditions, cell-based disease models, in particular induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) and standard transmitochondrial cybrids, have become useful tools for studying disease mechanisms, simulating mutation-specific phenotypes, and assessing possible therapeutic interventions. This review provides the key roles of mutations and oxidative stress in the pathogenesis of the disease in the context of the primary role of the mitochondrial genome, its maternal inheritance, and the most common disorders, i.e., mitochondrial encephalomyopathy, lactic acidosis, and stroke-like episodes (MELAS) and myoclonic epilepsy with ragged red fibers (MERRF). We outline the use of cell-based models to study mitochondrial pathologies, including patient-derived primary cells and iPSCs, which could be differentiated into cell types of interest to the disease, and cybrid systems, which could isolate the contribution of single mutations in the mitochondrial DNA to an underlying background of controlled nuclear genetic backgrounds. Besides, the review focuses on innovative technologies to mend mutations in mitochondrial DNA, such as allotopic expression, mitoTALENs and mitoZFNs, and the new base-editing systems like DdCBEs. Included are the free cell-based therapies like mitochondrial transfer and nuclear transfer procedures. Finally, we discussed the measures to be taken to minimize oxidative stress, and these actions are standard: mitochondria- targeted antioxidants, mitophagy, and autophagy regulation. The study also looks at the present level of proof supporting these therapy techniques and discusses the advantages and disadvantages of existing experimental models. Although several gene editing and mitochondria replacement technologies have shown promising results in clinical and cellular research, their clinical translation is still restricted and needs more confirmation in terms of long-term therapeutic efficacy, safety, and delivery efficiency.

item.title: Hydrogel-extracellular vesicle platforms: orchestrating the osteogenic microenvironment for cell-free bone regeneration.
item.abstract: Bone defects remain difficult to treat because impaired vascularization, inflammation, infection and metabolic dysfunction limit endogenous repair. Unencapsulated extracellular vesicles (EVs) may also be rapidly cleared from defect sites. Hydrogel-EV systems combine vesicle bioactivity with local retention, controlled release and structural support, offering a cell-free strategy for bone regeneration. This review summarizes EV sources, separation, characterization and cargo, and outlines the endosomal biogenesis of exosomes. We examine EV-mediated regulation of osteogenesis, angiogenesis, immunity and osteoclast-mediated resorption. Hydrogel materials, EV-loading approaches, passive and stimuli-responsive release, and methods for evaluating EVs within hydrogels are discussed. Applications in uncomplicated, infected and diabetes-associated bone defects are compared according to their pathological microenvironments. Translational barriers include heterogeneous EV preparations, inconsistent separation and dosing standards, inadequate mechanical performance, and mismatched hydrogel degradation and bone-healing kinetics. Insufficient biodistribution and long-term safety data further limit clinical translation. This review provides a framework for developing hydrogel-EV platforms for bone regeneration.

item.title: Mesenchymal stem cell-derived extracellular vesicles in diabetes: immunomodulation and therapeutic prospects.
item.abstract: Diabetes mellitus is characterized by chronic hyperglycemia, immune dysregulation, and progressive multi-organ injury. Mesenchymal stem cell-derived extracellular vesicles(MSC-EVs) have emerged as cell-free mediators capable of transferring bioactive cargo and modulating immune, metabolic, and regenerative responses. This narrative review summarizes current evidence on the roles of MSC-EVs in diabetes, focusing on immune-cell regulation, pancreatic β-cell protection, metabolic homeostasis, and major complications, while also considering EV isolation, engineering, delivery, and clinical translation. Preclinical studies indicate that MSC-EVs can modulate T-cell, macrophage, dendritic-cell, B-cell, natural killer-cell, innate lymphoid-cell, and complement-associated responses; reduce inflammatory and oxidative injury; protect β cells from apoptosis; improve insulin signaling; and promote tissue repair in diabetic wounds, kidney disease, retinopathy, neuropathy, cardiovascular injury, bone metabolic disorders, and erectile dysfunction. These effects are mediated by preparation-specific cargo and signaling pathways, including miRNAs, proteins, programmed death-ligand 1(PD-L1)/PD-1 signaling, Phosphoinositide 3-kinase/Protein Kinase B(PI3K/Akt)-related pathways, and phosphatase and tensin homolog(PTEN)/AKT signaling. The review also distinguishes direct diabetes-specific evidence from mechanistic background derived from non-diabetic models. However, the evidence remains heterogeneous across MSC sources, EV preparations, experimental models, doses, and delivery strategies, and current clinical evidence is still limited. Registered investigations should therefore be distinguished from studies reporting clinical outcomes, and product-specific efficacy should not be inferred from trial registration alone. Overall, MSC-EVs represent a promising but not yet established therapeutic platform for diabetes. Future translation will require standardized terminology and characterization, scalable manufacturing, reproducible potency assessment, optimized targeting and dosing, long-term safety evaluation, and well-designed product-specific clinical trials.

item.title: Residual Invasive Disease After Neoadjuvant Therapy in Triple-Negative Breast Cancer: Risk Stratification and Postoperative Radiotherapy-Pembrolizumab Integration.
item.abstract: Residual invasive disease (RD) after neoadjuvant systemic therapy identifies patients with triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) at increased but heterogeneous recurrence risk. Continued perioperative pembrolizumab may overlap with postoperative radiotherapy (RT), raising unresolved questions about treatment timing and long-term net clinical benefit. This narrative review examines the pathologic definition and distribution of RD, prognostic stratification, mechanistic evidence, and clinical studies of postoperative RT-pembrolizumab integration. Breast-only, nodal-only, and combined breast and nodal RD should be distinguished alongside residual burden. Residual cancer burden, nodal status, tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes, and circulating tumor DNA may inform prognosis or research stratification, but none is validated to predict benefit from a specific RT-pembrolizumab schedule. Longitudinal molecular monitoring and cell-free DNA fragmentomics remain investigational for postoperative treatment selection. DNA repair, hypoxia, metabolic adaptation, tumor-cell plasticity, and immune suppression provide plausible mechanisms of resistance. However, features measured in surgically removed RD cannot be assumed to persist in occult postoperative disease, and much of the supporting evidence is preclinical or derived from other treatment settings. RT may stimulate antitumor immunity while also injuring immune cells. Small nonrandomized postoperative studies support short-term feasibility of concurrent treatment, but do not establish comparative efficacy or long-term safety. Severe adverse events and treatment interruptions have occurred, and late cardiopulmonary injury, fibrosis, and reconstruction outcomes remain insufficiently characterized. Management should preserve timely, guideline-concordant RT and base pembrolizumab continuation or interruption on clinical recovery and toxicity. Prospective comparisons with clearly defined schedules, prespecified RD subgroups, biomarker analyses, and adequate follow-up are needed to establish long-term net clinical benefit.
